entries.f68e7d0c5aae22406c72547c7e3b887f568d43b7: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.10">Pro 30:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.10">10</reference> Calumniate not a servant with his master,      Lest he curse thee, and thou must atone for it. <div eID="gen11936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11937" type="x-p"/> Incorrectly Ewald: entice not a servant to slander against his master; and Hitzig: “Make not a servant tattle regarding his master.” It is true that the <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> לושׁן (to pierce with the tongue, <hi type="italic">linguâ petere</hi>) occurs twice in the sense of to calumniate; but that הלשׁין means nothing else, is attested by the post-bibl. Hebrew; the proverb regarding schismatics (בּרכּת המּינים) in the Jewish <hi type="italic">Schemone-Esre</hi> (prayer of the eighteen benedictions) began with ולמלשינים, “and to the calumniators” (<hi type="italic">delatoribus</hi>). Also in the Arab. âlsana signifies <hi type="italic">pertulit verba alicujus ad alterum</hi>, to make a babbler, <hi type="italic">rapporteur</hi> (Fleischer). That the word also here is not to be otherwise interpreted, is to be concluded from אל with the causative rendering. Rightly Symmachus, μὴ διαβάλῃς; Theodotion, μὴ καταλαλήσῃς; and according to the sense also, Jerome, <hi type="italic">ne accuses</hi>; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. μὴ καταμηνύσῃς (give not him); on the contrary, Luther, <hi type="italic">verrate nicht</hi> [betray not], renders הלשׁין with the lxx, Syr. in the sense of the Aram. אשׁלם and the Arab. âslam (<hi type="italic">tradere, prodere</hi>). One should not secretly accuse (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>) a servant with his master, and in that lies the character of slander (לשׁון הרע) when one puts suspicion upon him, or exaggerates the actual facts, and generally makes the person suspected - one thereby makes a man, whose lot in itself is not a happy one, at length and perhaps for ever unhappy, and thereby he brings a curse on himself. But it is no matter of indifference to be the object of the curse of a man whom one has unrighteously and unjustly overwhelmed in misery: such a curse is not without its influence, for it does not fruitlessly invoke the righteous retribution of God, and thus one has sorrowfully to atone for the wanton sins of the tongue (veaschāmta, for ve-aschamtá as it is would be without pause).
entries.243f2cc9b7a76f5e90b2adab6e14ad4fb96d169a: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.11-Prov.30.14">Pro 30:11-14</reference> <div eID="gen11937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11938" type="x-p"/> There now follows a <hi type="italic">Priamel</hi>,<note placement="foot">Cf. vol. i. p. 13. The name (from <hi type="italic">praeambulum</hi>) given to a peculiar form of popular gnomic poetry which prevailed in Germany from the 12th (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Meistersinger or Minstrel Sparvogel) to the 16th century, but was especially cultivated during the 14th and 15th centuries. Its peculiarity consisted in this, that after a series of antecedents or subjects, a briefly-expressed consequent or predicate was introduced as the epigrammatic point applicable to all these antecedents together. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Erschenburg’s <hi type="italic">Denkmälern altdeutscher Dichtkinst</hi>, Bremen 1799.</note> the first line of which is, by יקלל, connected with the יקללך of the preceding distich: 11 A generation that curseth their father,      And doth not bless their mother; 12 A generation pure in their own eyes,      And yet not washed from their filthiness; 13 A generation - how haughty their eyes,      And their eyelids lift themselves up; 14 A generation whose teeth are swords and their jaw teeth knives      To devour the poor from the earth and the needy from the midst of men. <div eID="gen11938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11939" type="x-p"/> Ewald translates: O generation! but that would have required the word, 13a, הדּור (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jer 2:31</reference>), and one would have expected to have found something mentioned which the generation addressed were to take heed to; but it is not so. But if “O generation!” should be equivalent to “O regarding the generation!” then הוי ought to have introduced the sentence. And if we translate, with Luther: There is a generation, etc., then ישׁ is supplied, which might drop out, but could not be omitted. The lxx inserts after ἔκγονον the word κακόν, and then renders what follows as pred. - a simple expedient, but worthless. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. does not need this expedient, for it renders γενεὰ τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ βλασφημέσει; but then the order of the words in 11a would have been דור יקלל אביו; and in 12a, after the manner of a subst. clause, דור טהור בעיניו הוא, one sees distinctly, from <reference osisRef="Prov.30.13">Pro 30:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pro 30:14</reference>, that what follows דור is to be understood, not as a pred., but as an attributive clause. As little can we interpret <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pro 30:14</reference>, with Löwenstein, as pred. of the three subj., “it is a generation whose teeth are swords;” that would at least have required the words דור הוא; but <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pro 30:14</reference> is not at all a judgment valid for all the three subjects. The Targ. and Jerome translate correctly, as we above;<note placement="foot">The Syr. begins 11a as if הוי were to be supplied.</note> but by this rendering there are four subjects in the preamble, and the whole appears, since the common pred. is wanting, as a mutilated Priamel. Perhaps the author meant to say: it is such a generation that encompasses us; or: such is an abomination to Jahve; for דור is a <hi type="italic">Gesamtheit</hi> = totality, generation of men who are bound together by contemporary existence, or homogeneity, or by both, but always a totality; so that these <reference osisRef="Prov.30.11-Prov.30.14">Pro 30:11-14</reference>, might describe <hi type="italic">quatuor detestabilia genera hominum</hi> (C. B. Michaelis), and yet one <hi type="italic">generatio</hi>, which divide among themselves these four vices, of blackest ingratitude, loathsome self-righteousness, arrogant presumption, and unmerciful covetousness. Similar is the description given in the Mishna <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> ix. 14, of the character of the age in which the Messiah appeared. “The appearance of this age,” thus it concludes, “is like the appearance of a dog; a son is not ashamed before his father; to whom will we then look for help? To our Father in heaven!”<note placement="foot">Cf. also Ali b. Abi Tâleb’s dark description, beginning with hadha alzman (this age), <hi type="italic">Zur allg. Char. der arab. Poesie</hi> (1870), p. 54f.</note> <div eID="gen11939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11940" type="x-p"/> The undutifulness of a child is here placed first. To curse one’s parents is, after <reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exo 21:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference>, a crime worthy of death; “not to bless,” is here, <hi type="italic">per litoten</hi>, of the same force as קלּל to curse. The second characteristic, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.12">Pro 30:12</reference>, is wicked blindness as to one’s judgment of himself. The lxx coarsely, but not bad: τὴν δ ̓ ἔξοδον αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἀπένιψεν. Of such darkness one says: <hi type="italic">sordes suas putat olere cinnama</hi>. רחץ is not the abbreviated part. (Stuart), as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>, but the finite, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hos 1:6. <div eID="gen11940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11941" type="x-p"/> In 13a the attributive clause forms itself, so as to express the astonishing height of arrogance, into an exclamation: a generation, how lofty are their eyes (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">Pro 6:17</reference>, עינים רמות)! to which, as usual, it is simply added: and his eyelids (<hi type="italic">palpebrae</hi>) lift themselves up; in Lat., the lifting up of the eyebrow as an expression of haughtiness is described by <hi type="italic">elatum</hi> (<hi type="italic">superbum</hi>) <hi type="italic">supercilium</hi>. <div eID="gen11941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11942" type="x-p"/> The fourth characteristic is insatiable covetousness, which does not spare even the poor, and preys upon them, the helpless and the defenceless: they devour them as one eats bread, Psa 14:4. The teeth, as the instruments of eating, are compared to swords and knives, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference> to spears and arrows. With שׁנּיו there is interchanged, as at <reference osisRef="Job.29.17">Job 29:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.6">Jon 1:6</reference>, מתלּעתיו (not 'מת, as Norzi writes, contrary to <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>-<hi type="italic">Setzung</hi>, §37, according to which <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, with the servant going before, is inadmissible), transposed from מלתּעתיו, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.7">Psa 58:7</reference>, from לתע, to strike, pierce, bite. The designation of place, מארץ, “from the earth” (which also, <hi type="italic">in pausa</hi>, is not modified into מארץ), and מאדם, “from the midst of men,” do not belong to the obj.: those who belong to the earth, to mankind (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Psa 10:18</reference>), for thus interpreted they would be useless; but to the word of action: from the earth, out from the midst of men away, so that they disappear from thence (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.4">Amo 8:4</reference>). By means of fine but cobweb combinations, Hitzig finds Amalek in this fourfold proverb. But it is a portrait of the times, like <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, and certainly without any national stamp.
entries.c20407c8fc9a7d24c9350b2698d7587721e43250: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15-Prov.30.16">Pro 30:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen11942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11943" type="x-p"/> With the characteristic of insatiableness <reference osisRef="Prov.30.11-Prov.30.14">Pro 30:11-14</reference> closes, and there follows an <hi type="italic">apophthegma de quatuor insatiabilibus quae ideo comparantur cum sanguisuga</hi> (C. B. Michaelis). We translate the text here as it lies before us: 15 The ‛Alûka hath two daughters: Give! Give!      Three of these are never satisfied;      Four say not: Enough! 16 The under-world and the closing of the womb;      The earth is not satisfied with water;      And the fire saith not: Enough! <div eID="gen11943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11944" type="x-p"/> We begin with Masoretic externalities. The first ב in הב is <hi type="italic">Beth minusculum</hi>; probably it had accidentally this diminutive form in the original MSS, to which the Midrash (cf. <hi type="italic">Sepher Taghin ed. Bargès</hi>, 1866, p. 47) has added absurd conceits. This first הב has <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after it, which in this case is servant to the <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> going before, according to the rule <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 24, here, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">Psa 85:9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Mehuppach</hi>. The second הב, which of itself alone is the representative of <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, has in Hutter, as in the Cod. Erfurt 2, and Cod. 2 of the Leipzig Public Library, the pausal punctuation הב (cf. קח, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10">1Sa 21:10</reference>), but which is not sufficiently attested. Instead of לא־אמרוּ, 15b, לא אמרוּ, and instead of לא־אמרה f, 16b, לא אמרה are to be written; the <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi> removes the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, according to <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 9, <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, iv. §2. Instead of מים, 16a, only Jablonski, as Mühlau remarks, has מים; but incorrectly, since <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, after <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, has no pausal force (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 37). All that is without any weight as to the import of the words. But the punctuation affords some little service for the setting aside of a view of Rabbenu Tam (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Tosaphoth</hi> to <hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi> 17a, and <hi type="italic">Erubin</hi> 19a), which has been lately advocated by Löwenstein. That view is, that ‛Alûka is the name of a wise man, not Solomon’s, because the Pesikta does not reckon this among the names of Solomon, nor yet a name of hell, because it is not, in the Gemara, numbered among the names of Gehinnom. Thus לעלוּקה would be a superscription, like לדוד and לשׁלמה, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference>, provided with <hi type="italic">Asla Legarmeh</hi>. But this is not possible, for the <hi type="italic">Asla Legarmeh</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference>, is the transformation of <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, inadmissible on the first word of the verse (<hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xix. §1); but no <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> can follow such an <hi type="italic">Asla Legarmeh</hi>, which has the force of an <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>, as after this לעלוקה, which the accentuation then does not regard as the author’s name given as a superscription. עלוּקה is not the name of a person, and generally not a proper name, but a generic name of certain traditional signification. “One must drink no water” - says the Gemara <hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi> 12b - “out of a river or pond, nor (immediately) with his mouth, nor by means of his hand; he who, nevertheless, does it, his blood comes on his own head, because of the danger. What danger? סכּנת עלוּקה,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the danger of swallowing a leech. The Aram. also designates a leech by עלוּקא (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Targ. Ps. 12:9: hence the godless walk about like the leech, which sucks the blood of men), and the Arab. by 'alaḳ (<hi type="italic">n. unit</hi>. 'alaḳat), as the word is also rendered here by the Aram. and Arab. translators. Accordingly, all the Greeks render it by βδέλλη; Jerome, by <hi type="italic">sanguisuga</hi> (Rashi, <hi type="italic">sangsue</hi>); also Luther’s <hi type="italic">Eigel</hi> is not the <hi type="italic">Igel erinaceus</hi> [hedgehog], but the <hi type="italic">Egel</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as we now designate it, the <hi type="italic">Blutegel</hi> [leech], or (less correctly) <hi type="italic">Blutigel</hi>. עלוּקה is the fem. of the adj. עלוּק, attached to, which meaning, together with the whole verbal stem, the Arab. has preserved (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Mühlau’s <hi type="italic">Mittheilung des Art. 'aluka aus dem Kamus</hi>, p. 42).<note placement="foot">Nöldeke has remarked, with reference to Mühlau’s <hi type="italic">Monographie</hi>, that ‛aluḳa, in the sense of tenacious (<hi type="italic">tenax</hi>), is also found in Syr. (<hi type="italic">Geopon</hi>. xiii. 9, xli. 26), and that generally the stem עלק, to cleave, to adhere, is more common in Aram. than one would suppose. But this, however common in Arab., is by no means so in Syr.; and one may affirm that, among other Arabisms found in the Proverbs of Agur, the word ‛Alûka has decidedly an Arab. sound.</note> <div eID="gen11944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11945" type="x-p"/> But if, now, the ‛Alûka is the leech,<note placement="foot">In Sanscrit the leech is called galaukas (masc.) or galaukâ (fem.), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the inhabitant of the water (from gala, water, and ôkas, dwelling). Ewald regards this as a transformation of the Semitic name.</note> which are then its two daughters, to which is here given the name הב הב, and which at the same time have this cry of desire in their mouths? Grotius and others understand, by the two daughters of the leech, the two branches of its tongue; more correctly: the double-membered overlip of its sucker. C. B. Michaelis thinks that the greedy cry, “Give! Give!” is personified: <hi type="italic">voces istae concipiuntur ut hirudinis filiae, quas ex se gignat et velut mater sobolem impense diligat</hi>. But since this does not satisfy, symbolical interpretations of ‛Aluka have been resorted to. The Talmud, <hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi> 17a, regards it as a name of hell. In this sense it is used in the language of the Pijut (synagogue poetry).<note placement="foot">So says <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Salomo ha-Babli, in a <hi type="italic">Zulath</hi> of the first <hi type="italic">Chanukka-Sabbats</hi> (beginning אין צוּר חלף): יקדוּ כּהבהבי עלק, they burn like the flames of hell.</note> <div eID="gen11945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11946" type="x-p"/> If ‛Alûka is hell, then fancy has the widest room for finding an answer to the question, What are the two daughters? The Talmud supposes that רשׁות (the worldly domination) and מינות (heresy) are meant. The Church-fathers also, understanding by ‛Alûka the power of the devil, expatiated in such interpretations. Of the same character are Calmet’s interpretation, that <hi type="italic">sanguisuga</hi> is a figure of the <hi type="italic">mala cupiditas</hi>, and its twin-daughters are <hi type="italic">avaritia</hi> and <hi type="italic">ambitio</hi>. The truth lying in all these is this, that here there must be some kind of symbol. But if the poet meant, by the two daughters of the ‛Alûka, two beings or things which he does not name, then he kept the best of his symbol to himself. And could he use ‛Alûka, this common name for the leech, without further intimation, in any kind of symbolical sense? The most of modern interpreters do nothing to promote the understanding of the word, for they suppose that ‛Alûka, from its nearest signification, denotes a demoniacal spirit of the character of a vampire, like the <hi type="italic">Dakinî</hi> of the Indians, which nourish themselves on human flesh; the ghouls of the Arabs and Persians, which inhabit graveyards, and kill and eat men, particularly wanderers in the desert; in regard to which it is to be remarked, that (Arab.) ‛awlaḳ is indeed a name for a demon, and that al‛aluwaḳ, according to the Kamus, is used in the sense of alghwal. Thus Dathe, Döderlein, Ziegler, Umbreit; thus also Hitzig, Ewald, and others. Mühlau, while he concurs in this understanding of the word, and now throwing open the question, Which, then, are the two daughters of the demoness ‛Alûka? finds no answer to it in the proverb itself, and therefore accepts of the view of Ewald, since 15b-16, taken by themselves, form a fully completed whole, that the line 'לעלוקה וגו is the beginning of a numerical proverb, the end of which is wanting. We acknowledge, because of the obscurity - not possibly aimed at by the author himself - in which the two daughters remain, the fragmentary characters of the proverb of the ‛Alûka; Stuart also does this, for he regards it as brought out of a connection in which it was intelligible - but we believe that the line 'שׁלושׁ וגו is an original formal part of this proverb. For the proverb forming, according to Mühlau’s judgment, a whole rounded off: שׁלושׁ הנה לא תשׂבענה ארבע לא אמרו הון שׁאול ועצר רחם ארץ לא שׂבעה מים ואשׁ לא אמרה הון contains a mark which makes the original combination of these five lines improbable. Always where the third is exceeded by the fourth, the step from the third to the fourth is taken by the connecting <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18">Pro 30:18</reference>, וארבע; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.21">Pro 30:21</reference>, ותחת ארבע; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.29">Pro 30:29</reference>, וארבעה. We therefore conclude that 'ארבע לא וגו is the original commencement of independent proverb. This proverb is: <div eID="gen11946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11947" type="x-p"/> Four things say not: Enough! <div eID="gen11947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11948" type="x-p"/> The under-world and the closing of the womb [i.e., unfruitful womb] - <div eID="gen11948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11949" type="x-p"/> The earth is not satisfied with water, <div eID="gen11949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11950" type="x-p"/> And the fire says not: Enough! a tetrastich more acceptable and appropriate than the Arab. proverb (Freytag, <hi type="italic">Provv</hi>. iii. p. 61, No. 347): “three things are not satisfied by three: the womb, and wood by fire, and the earth by rain;” and, on the other hand, it is remarkable to find it thus clothed in the Indian language,<note placement="foot">That not only natural productions, but also ideas and literary productions (words, proverbs, knowledge), were conveyed from the Indians to the Semites, and from the Semites to the Indians, on the great highways by sea and land, is a fact abundantly verified. There is not in this, however, any means of determining the situation of Massa.</note> as given in the Hitopadesa (p. 67 of Lassen’s ed.), and in Pantschatantra, i. 153 (ed. of Kosegarten): nâgnis tṛpjati kâshṭhânân nâpagânân mahôdadhih nântakah sarvabhûtânân na punsân vâmalocanâh. <div eID="gen11950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11951" type="x-p"/> Fire is not sated with wood, nor the ocean with the streams, <div eID="gen11951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11952" type="x-p"/> Nor death with all the living, nor the beautiful-eyed with men. <div eID="gen11952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11953" type="x-p"/> As in the proverb of Agur the 4 falls into 2 + 2, so also in this Indian <hi type="italic">sloka</hi>. In both, fire and the realm of death (ântaka is death as the personified “end-maker”) correspond; and as there the womb and the earth, so here <hi type="italic">feminarium cupiditas</hi> and the ocean. The parallelizing of ארץ and רחם is after passages such as <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference> (cf. also <reference osisRef="Prov.5.16">Pro 5:16</reference>; Num 24:7; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa 48:1</reference>); that of שׁאול and אשׁ is to be judged of<note placement="foot">The parallelizing of רחם and שׁאול, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 15b, is not directly aimed at by the poet.</note> after passages such as <reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">Deu 32:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.12">Isa 56:1-12</reference> :24. That לא אמרו הון repeats itself in לא אמרה הון is now, as we render the proverb independently, much more satisfactory than if it began with 'שׁלושׁ וגו: it rounds itself off, for the end returns into the beginning. Regarding הון, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 1:13. From הוּן, to be light, it signifies living lightly; ease, superabundance, in that which renders life light or easy. “Used accusatively, and as an exclamation, it is equivalent to plenty! enough! It is used in the same sense in the North African Arab. brrakat (spreading out, fulness). Wetzstein remarks that in Damascus lahôn <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, hitherto, is used in the sense of ḥajah, enough; and that, accordingly, we may attempt to explain הון of our Heb. language in the sense of (Arab.) hawn haddah, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, here the end of it!” (Mühlau). <div eID="gen11953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11954" type="x-p"/> But what do we now make of the two remaining lines of the proverb of the ‛Alûka? The proverb also in this division of two lines is a fragment. Ewald completes it, for to the one line, of which, according to his view, the fragment consists, he adds two: <div eID="gen11954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11955" type="x-p"/> The bloodsucker has two daughters, “Hither! hither!” <div eID="gen11955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11956" type="x-p"/> Three saying, “Hither, hither, hither the blood, <div eID="gen11956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11957" type="x-p"/> The blood of the wicked child.” <div eID="gen11957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11958" type="x-p"/> A proverb of this kind may stand in the O.T. alone: it sounds as if quoted from Grimm’s <hi type="italic">Mährchen</hi>, and is a side-piece to Zappert’s <hi type="italic">altdeutsch. Schlummerliede</hi>. Cannot the mutilation of the proverb be rectified in a less violent way without any self-made addition? If this is the case, that in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pro 30:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.30.16">Pro 30:16</reference>, which now form one proverb, there are two melted together, only the first of which lies before us in a confused form, then this phenomenon is explained by supposing that the proverb of the ‛Alûka originally stood in this form: <div eID="gen11958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11959" type="x-p"/> The ‛Alûka has two daughters: Give! give! - <div eID="gen11959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11960" type="x-p"/> The under-world and the closing of the womb; <div eID="gen11960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11961" type="x-p"/> There are three that are never satisfied. <div eID="gen11961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11962" type="x-p"/> Thus completed, this tristich presents itself as the original side-piece of the lost tetrastich, beginning with ארבע. One might suppose that if שׁאול and עצר רחם have to be regarded as the daughters of the ‛Alûka, which Hitzig and also Zöckler have recognised, then there exists no reason for dividing the one proverb into two. Yet the taking of them as separate is necessary, for this reason, because in the fourth, into which it expands, the ‛Alûka is altogether left out of account. But in the above tristich it is taken into account, as was to be expected, as the mother with her children. This, that sheol (שׁאול is for the most part fem.), and the womb (רחם = רחם, which is fem., <reference osisRef="Jer.20.17">Jer 20:17</reference>) to which conception is denied, are called, on account of their greediness, the daughters of the ‛Alûka, is to be understood in the same way as when a mountain height is called, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>, a horn of the son of oil. In the Arab., which is inexhaustibly rich in such figurative names, a man is called “a son of the clay (limi);” a thief, “a son of the night;” a nettle, “the daughter of fire.” The under-world and a closed womb have the ‛Alûka nature; they are insatiable, like the leech. It is unnecessary to interpret, as Zöckler at last does, ‛Alûka as the name of a female demon, and the לילית, “daughters,” as her companions. It may be adduced in favour of this view that לעלוּקה is without the article, after the manner of a proper name. But is it really without the article? Such a doubtful case we had before us at Pro 27:23. As yet only Böttcher, §394, has entered on this difficulty of punctuation. We compare <reference osisRef="Gen.29.27">Gen 29:27</reference>, בּעבדה; 1Ki 12:32, לעגלים; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.7">1Ch 13:7</reference>, בּעגלה; and consequently also <reference osisRef="Ps.146.7">Psa 146:7</reference>, לעשׁוּקים; thus the assimilating force of the <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi> appears here to have changed the syntactically required ל and בּ into ל and בּ. But also supposing that עלוּקה in לעלוּקה is treated as a proper name, this is explained from the circumstance that the leech is not meant here in the natural history sense of the word, but as embodied greediness, and is made a person, one individual being. Also the symbol of the two daughters is opposed to the mythological character of the ‛Alûka. The imper. הב, from יהב, occurs only here and at <reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Dan 7:17</reference> (= תּן), and in the bibl. Heb. only with the intentional āh, and in inflection forms. The insatiableness of sheol (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pro 27:20</reference>) is described by Isa; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>; and Rachel, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Gen 30:1</reference>, with her “Give me children,” is an example of the greediness of the “closed-up womb” (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.18">Gen 20:18</reference>). The womb of a childless wife is meant, which, because she would have children, the <hi type="italic">nuptiae</hi> never satisfy; or also of one who, because she does not fear to become pregnant, invites to her many men, and always burns anew with lust. “In Arab. 'aluwaḳ means not only one fast bound to her husband, but, according to Wetzstein, in the whole of Syria and Palestine, the prostitute, as well as the κίναιδοι, are called 'ulak (plur. 'alwak), because they obtrude themselves and hold fast to their victim” (Mühlau). In the third line, the three: the leech, hell, and the shut womb, are summarized: <hi type="italic">tira sunt quae non satiantur</hi>. Thus it is to be translated with Fleischer, not with Mühlau and others, <hi type="italic">tira haec non satiantur</hi>. “These three” is expressed in Heb. by שׁלשׁ־אלּה, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.11">Exo 21:11</reference>, or אלּה(ה) שׁלשׁת, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.22">2Sa 21:22</reference>; הנּה (which, besides, does not signify <hi type="italic">haec</hi>, but <hi type="italic">illa</hi>) is here, taken correctly, the pred., and represents in general the verb of being (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Isa 51:19</reference>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 6:16. Zöckler finds the point of the proverb in the greediness of the unfruitful womb, and is of opinion that the poet purposely somewhat concealed this point, and gave to his proverb thereby the enhanced attraction of the ingenious. But the tetrastich 'אברע וגו shows that hell, which is compared to fire, and the unfruitful womb, to which the parched and thirsty earth is compared, were placed by the poet on one and the same line; it is otherwise with <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18-Prov.30.20">Pro 30:18-20</reference>, but where that point is nothing less than concealed.
entries.c3c8d4e6e602cd713315abc8c26cda4fa2d672a2: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">Pro 30:17</reference> <div eID="gen11962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11963" type="x-p"/> The proverb of the ‛Alûka is the first of the proverbs founded on the figure of an animal among the “words” of Agur. It is now followed by another of a similar character: 17 An eye that mocketh at his father,      And despiseth obedience to his mother:      The ravens of the brook shall pluck it out,      And the young eagles shall eat it. <div eID="gen11963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11964" type="x-p"/> If “an eye,” and not “eyes,” are spoken of here, this is accounted for by the consideration that the duality of the organ falls back against the unity of the mental activity and mental expression which it serves (cf. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 234). As haughtiness reveals itself (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.13">Pro 30:13</reference>) in the action of the eyes, so is the eye also the mirror of humble subordination, and also of malicious scorn which refuses reverence and subjection to father and mother. As in German the verbs [<hi type="italic">verspotten, spotten, höhnen, hohnsprechen</hi> signifying to mock at or scorn may be used with the accus., genit., or dat., so also לעג [to deride] and בּוּז [to despise] may be connected at pleasure with either an accusative object or a dative object. Ben-Chajim, Athias, van der Hooght, and others write תּלעג; Jablonski, Michaelis, Löwenstein, תּלעג, Mühlau, with Norzi, accurately, תּלעג, with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, like תּבחר, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>; the writing of Ben-Asher<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> has its reason in the <hi type="italic">Zinnor</hi> that follows, and the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> in the syllable beginning with a moveable <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi>; תּלעג with <hi type="italic">Scheva quiesc</hi>. must, according to rule, receive <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 26.</note> is תּלעג, with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>. The punctuation of ליקהת is more fluctuating. The word לקהת (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>.) may remain out of view, for the <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi> in ק stands here as firmly as at <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, cf. Psa 45:10. But it is a question whether one has to write ליקּהת with <hi type="italic">Yod quiesc</hi>. (regarding this form of writing, preferred by Ben-Naphtali, the <hi type="italic">Psalmen-Comm</hi>. under <reference osisRef="Ps.45.10">Psa 45:10</reference>, in both Edd.; Luzzatto’s <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §193; Baer’s <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 84, note 2; and Heidenheim’s <hi type="italic">Pentateuch</hi>, with the text-crit. <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>. of Jekuthiël ha-Nakdans, under <reference osisRef="Gen.47.17">Gen 47:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>), as it is found in Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 45a, and under יקה, and as also Norzi requires, or ליקּהת (as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Cod. Erfurt 1), which appears to be the form adopted by Ben-Asher, for it is attested<note placement="foot">Kimchi is here no authority, for he contradicts himself regarding such word-forms. Thus, regarding ויללת, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.36">Jer 25:36</reference>, in <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 87b, and under ילל. The form also wavers between כּיתרון and כּיתרון, Ecc 2:13. The Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>. has here the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> always <hi type="italic">quiesc</hi>.</note> as such by Jekuthiël under <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, and also expressly as such by an old Masora-Cod. of the Erfurt Library. Löwenstein translates, “the weakness of the mother.” Thus after Rashi, who refers the word to קהה, to draw together, and explains it, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, “collection;” but in the passage before us, understands it of the wrinkles on the countenance of the aged mother. Nachmani (Ramban) goes still further, giving to the word, at <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, everywhere the meaning of weakness and frailty. Aben Ezra also, and Gersuni (Ralbag), do not go beyond the meaning of a drawing together; and the lxx, with the Aram., who all translate the word by <hi type="italic">senectus</hi>, have also קהה in the sense of to become dull, infirm (certainly not the Aethiopic leheḳa, to become old, weak through old age). But Kimchi, whom the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. and Luther<note placement="foot">Jerome translates, <hi type="italic">et qui despicit partum matris suae</hi>. To <hi type="italic">partus</hi> there separates itself to him here the signification <hi type="italic">expectatio</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, resting on a false combination with קוה. To think of <hi type="italic">pareo, parui, paritum</hi> (Mühlau), was not yet granted to him.</note> follow, is informed by Abulwalîd, skilled in the Arab., of a better: יקהה (or יקּהה, cf. נצּרה, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference>) is the Arab. wakhat, obedience (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., above יקה under 1a). If now it is said of such a haughty, insolent eye, that the ravens of the brook (cf. 1Ki 17:4) will pluck it out, and the בני־נשׁר eat it, they, the eagle’s children, the unchildlike human eye: it is only the description of the fate that is before such an one, to die a violent death, and to become a prey to the fowls of heaven (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Jer 16:3., and Passow’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>. under κόραξ); and if this threatening is not always thus literally fulfilled, yet one has not on that account to render the future optatively, with Hitzig; this is a false conclusion, from a too literal interpretation, for the threatening is only to be understood after its spirit, viz., that a fearful and a dishonourable end will come to such an one. Instead of יקּרוּה, as Mühlau reads from the Leipzig Cod., יקרוה, with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> (Athias and Nissel have it with <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>), is to be read, for a word between <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> and <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> must always contain a conjunctive accent (<hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 51; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. §9). ערבי־נחל is also irregular, and instead of it ערבי־נחל is to be written, for the reason given above under <reference osisRef="Prov.30.16">Pro 30:16</reference> (מים).
entries.407f4b6525fd3d681302c102db15d0606093c188: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18-Prov.30.20">Pro 30:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen11964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11965" type="x-p"/> The following proverb, again a numerical proverb, begins with the eagle, mentioned in the last line of the foregoing: 18 Three things lie beyond me,      And four I understand not: 19 The way of the eagle in the heavens,      The way of a serpent over a rock,      The way of a ship on the high sea,      And the way of a man with a maid. 20 Thus is the way of the adulterous woman:      She eateth and wipeth her mouth, and saith:      I have done no iniquity. נפלאוּ ממּנּי, as relative clause, like 15b (where Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion rightly: τρία δέ ἐστιν ἃ οὐ πλησθήσεται), is joined to שׁלשׁה המּה. On the other hand, ארבע (τέσσαρα, for with the Kerı̂, conforming to 18a, ארבּעה, τέσσαρας) has to be interpreted as object. accus. The introduction of four things that are not known is in expressions like <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>; cf. Psa 139:6. The turning-point lies in the fourth; to that point the other three expressions gravitate, which have not an object in themselves, but are only as <hi type="italic">folie</hi> to the fourth. The articles wanting after הנּשׁר: they would be only the marks of the gender, and are therefore unnecessary; cf. under Pro 29:2. And while בּשּׁמים, in the heavens, and בלב־ים, in the sea, are the expressions used, עלי צוּר is used for on the rock, because here “on” is not at the same time “in,” “within,” as the eagle cleaves the air and the ship the waves. For this same reason the expression, “the way of a man בּעלמה,” is not to be understood of love unsought, suddenly taking possession of and captivating a man toward this or that maid, so that the principal thought of the proverb may be compared to the saying, “marriages are made in heaven;” but, as in <hi type="italic">Kidduschin</hi> 2b, with reference to this passage, is said <hi type="italic">coitus via appellatur</hi>. The ב refers to <hi type="italic">copula carnalis</hi>. But in what respect did his understanding not reach to this? “Wonderful,” thus Hitzig explains as the best interpreter of this opinion elsewhere (cf. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 115) propounded, “appeared to him the flying, and that how a large and thus heavy bird could raise itself so high in the air (<reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference>); then how, over the smooth rock, which offers no hold, the serpent pushes itself along; finally, how the ship in the trackless waves, which present nothing to the eye as a guide, nevertheless finds its way. These three things have at the same time this in common, that they leave no trace of their pathway behind them. But of the fourth way that cannot be said; for the trace is left on the <hi type="italic">substrat</hi>, which the man דּרך, and it becomes manifest, possibly as pregnancy, keeping out of view that the עלמה may yet be בתולה. That which is wonderful is consequently only the coition itself, its mystical act and its incomprehensible consequences.” But does not this interpretation carry in itself its own refutation? To the three wonderful ways which leave no traces behind them, there cannot be compared a fourth, the consequences of which are not only not trackless, but, on the contrary, become manifest as proceeding from the act in an incomprehensible way. The point of comparison is either the wonderfulness of the event or the tracklessness of its consequences. But now “the way of a man בתולה” is altogether inappropriate to designate the wonderful event of the origin of a human being. How altogether differently the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> expresses itself on this matter is seen from <reference osisRef="Job.10.8-Job.10.12">Job 10:8-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 210). That “way of a man with a maid” denotes only the act of coition, which physiologically differs in nothing from that of the lower animals, and which in itself, in the externality of its accomplishment, the poet cannot possibly call something transcendent. And why did he use the word בעלמה, and not rather בּנקבה [with a female] or בּאשּׁה [<hi type="italic">id</hi>.]? For this reason, because he meant the act of coition, not as a physiological event, but as a historical occurrence, as it takes place particularly in youth as the goal of love, not always reached in the divinely-appointed way. The point of comparison hence is not the secret of conception, but the tracelessness of the carnal intercourse. Now it is also clear why the way of the serpent עלי צור was in his eye: among grass, and still more in sand, the trace of the serpent’s path would perhaps be visible, but not on a hard stone, over which it has glided. And it is clear why it is said of the ship בלב־ים [in the heart of the sea]: while the ship is still in sight from the land, one knows the track it follows; but who can in the heart of the sea, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, on the high sea, say that here or there a ship has ploughed the water, since the water-furrows have long ago disappeared? Looking to the heavens, one cannot say that an eagle has passed there; to the rock, that a serpent has wound its way over it; to the high sea, that a ship has been steered through it; to the maid, that a man has had carnal intercourse with her. That the fact might appear on nearer investigation, although this will not always guide to a certain conclusion, is not kept in view; only the outward appearance is spoken of, the intentional concealment (Rashi) being in this case added thereto. Sins against the sixth [= seventh] commandment remain concealed from human knowledge, and are distinguished from others by this, that they shun human cognition (as the proverb says: אין אפיטרופוס לעריות, there is for sins of the flesh no ἐπίτροπος) - unchastity can mask itself, the marks of chastity are deceitful, here only the All-seeing Eye (עין ראה כּל, <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> ii. 1) perceives that which is done. Yet it is not maintained that “the way of a man with a maid” refers exclusively to external intercourse; but altogether on this side the proverb gains ethical significance. Regarding עלמה (from עלם, <hi type="italic">pubes esse et caeundi cupidus</hi>, not from עלם, to conceal, and not, as Schultens derives it, from עלם, <hi type="italic">signare</hi>, to seal) as distinguished from בּתוּלה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Isa 7:14. The mark of maidenhood belongs to עלמה not in the same way as to בתולה (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.24.43">Gen 24:43</reference> with 16), but only the marks of puberty and youth; the wife אשּׁה (viz., אושׁת אישׁ) cannot as such be called עלמה. Ralbag’s gloss עלמה שׁהיא בעולה is incorrect, and in Arama’s explanation (<hi type="italic">Akeda</hi>, Abschn. 9): the time is not to be determined when the sexual love of the husband to his wife flames out, ought to have been ודרך אישׁ בּאשׁתּו ne. One has therefore to suppose that <reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Pro 30:20</reference> explains what is meant by “the way of a man with a maid” by a strong example (for “the adulterous woman” can mean only an old adulteress), there not inclusive, for the tracklessness of sins of the flesh in their consequences. <div eID="gen11965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11966" type="x-p"/> This 20th verse does not appear to have been an original part of the numerical proverb, but is an appendix thereto (Hitzig). If we assume that כּן points forwards: thus as follows is it with the... (Fleischer), then we should hold this verse as an independent cognate proverb; but where is there a proverb (except <reference osisRef="Prov.11.19">Pro 11:19</reference>) that begins with כּן? כן, which may mean <hi type="italic">eodem modo</hi> (for one does not say כּן גּם) as well as <hi type="italic">eo modo</hi>, here points backwards in the former sense. Instead of וּמחתה פּיה (not פּיה; for the attraction of that which follows, brought about by the retrogression of the tone of the first word, requires dageshing, <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 30) the lxx has merely ἀπονιψαμένη, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as Immanuel explains: מקנּחה עצמה, <hi type="italic">abstergens semet ipsam</hi>, with Grotius, who to <hi type="italic">tergens os suum</hi> adds the remark: σεμνολογία (<hi type="italic">honesta elocutio</hi>). But eating is just a figure, like the “secret bread,” <reference osisRef="Prov.9.17">Pro 9:17</reference>, and the wiping of the mouth belongs to this figure. This appendix, with its כן, confirms it, that the intention of the four ways refers to the tracklessness of the consequences.
entries.30f3a3854bf7cc38c52c8235bcef1909f9bfa9f6: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.21-Prov.30.23">Pro 30:21-23</reference> <div eID="gen11966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11967" type="x-p"/> It is now not at all necessary to rack one’s brains over the grounds or the reasons of the arrangement of the following proverb (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Hitzig). There are, up to this point, two numerical proverbs which begin with שׁתּים, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.7">Pro 30:7</reference>, and שׁתּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pro 30:15</reference>; after the cipher 2 there then, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18">Pro 30:18</reference>, followed the cipher 3, which is now here continued: 21 Under three things doth the earth tremble,      And under four can it not stand: 22 Under a servant when he becomes king,      And a profligate when he has bread enough; 23 Under an unloved woman when she is married,      And a maid-servant when she becomes heiress to her mistress. <div eID="gen11967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11968" type="x-p"/> We cannot say here that the 4 falls into 3 + 1; but the four consists of four ones standing beside one another. ארץ is here without pausal change, although the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.30.24">Pro 30:24</reference>, where the modification of sound occurs, divides the verse into two; מארץ, 14b (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.2">Psa 35:2</reference>), remains, on the other hand, correctly unchanged. The “earth” stands here, as frequently, instead of the inhabitants of the earth. It trembles when one of the four persons named above comes and gains free space for acting; it feels itself oppressed as by an insufferable burden (an expression similar to <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10">Amo 7:10</reference>); - the arrangement of society is shattered; an oppressive closeness of the air, as it were, settles over all minds. The first case is already designated, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.10">Pro 19:10</reference>, as improper: under a slave, when he comes to reign (<hi type="italic">quum rex fit</hi>); for suppose that such an one has reached the place of government, not by the murder of the king and by the robbery of the crown, but, as is possible in an elective monarchy, by means of the dominant party of the people, he will, as a rule, seek to indemnify himself in his present highness for his former lowliness, and in the measure of his rule show himself unable to rise above his servile habits, and to pass out of the limited circle of his earlier state. The second case is this: a נבל, one whose mind is perverted and whose conduct is profligate - in short, a low man (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference>) - ישׂבּע־לחם (cf. <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>-<hi type="italic">Setzung</hi>, §28), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, has enough to eat (cf. to the expression <reference osisRef="Prov.28.19">Pro 28:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference>); for this undeserved living without care and without want makes him only so much the more arrogant, and troublesome, and dangerous. The שׂנוּאה, in the second case, is not thought of as a spouse, and that, as in supposed polygamy, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">Gen 29:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.15-Deut.21.17">Deu 21:15-17</reference>, as fallen into disfavour, but who again comes to favour and honour (Dathe, Rosenmüller); for she can be שׂנואה without her own fault, and as such she is yet no גּרוּשׁה; and it is not to be perceived why the re-assumption of such an one should shatter social order. Rightly Hitzig, and, after his example, Zöckler: an unmarried lady, an old spinster, is meant, whom no one desired because she had nothing attractive, and was only repulsive (cf. Grimm, under Sir. 7:26b). If such an one, as כּי תבעל says, at length, however, finds her husband and enters into the married relation, then she carries her head so much the higher; for she gives vent to ill-humour, strengthened by long restraint, against her subordinates; then she richly requites her earlier and happily married companions for their depreciation of her, among whom she had to suffer, as able to find no one who would love her. In the last case it is asked whether כּי־תירשׁ is meant of inheriting as an heiress (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Targ., Jerome, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther), or supplanting (Euchel, Gesenius, Hitzig), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, an entering into the inheritance of the dead, or an entering into the place of a living mistress. Since ירשׁ, with the accus. of the person, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.3-Gen.15.4">Gen 15:3-4</reference>, signifies to be the heir of one, and only with the accus. of peoples and lands signifies, “to take into possession (to seize) by supplanting,” the former is to be preferred; the lxx (Syr.), ὅταν ἐκβάλῃ, appear to have read כּי־תגרשׁ. This גּרשׁ would certainly be, after <reference osisRef="Gen.21.10">Gen 21:10</reference>, a piece of the world turned upside down; but also the entering, as heiress, into the inheritance, makes the maid-servant the reverse of that which she was before, and brings with it the danger that the heiress, notwithstanding her want of culture and dignity, demean herself also as heiress of the rank. Although the old Israelitish law knew only intestate succession to an inheritance, yet there also the case might arise, that where there were no natural or legal heirs, the bequest of a wife of rank passed over to her servants and nurses.
entries.5d2d2b44930cde4f185cfe0b9b5a101bfa0d01eb: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.24-Prov.30.28">Pro 30:24-28</reference> <div eID="gen11968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11969" type="x-p"/> Another proverb with the cipher 4, its first line terminating in ארץ: 24 Four are the little things of the earth,      And yet they are quick of wit - wise: 25 The ants - a people not strong,      And yet they prepare in summer their food; 26 Conies - a people not mighty,      And yet set their dwelling on the rocks; 27 No king have the locusts,      And yet they go forth in rank and file, all of them together; 28 The lizard thou canst catch with the hands,      And yet it is in the king’s palaces. <div eID="gen11969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11970" type="x-p"/> By the disjunctive accent, ארבּעה, in spite of the following word toned on the beginning, retains its <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-toning, 18a; but here, by the conjunctive accent, the tone retrogrades to the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., which does not elsewhere occur with this word. The connection קטנּי־ארץ is not superlat. (for it is impossible that the author could reckon the שׁפנים, conies, among the smallest of beasts), but, as in the expression נכבּדּי־ארץ, the honoured of the earth, Isa 23:8. In 24b, the lxx, Syr., Jerome, and Luther see in מ the comparative: σοφώτερα τῶν σοφῶν (מחכמים), but in this connection of words it could only be partitive (wise, reckoning among the wise); the <hi type="italic">part. Pual</hi> מחכּמים (Theodotion, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. σεσοφισμένα) was in use after <reference osisRef="Ps.88.6">Psa 88:6</reference>, and signified, like בּשׁל מבשּׁל, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.9">Exo 12:9</reference>, boiled well; thus חכמים מחכמים, taught wit, wise, cunning, prudent (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.64.7">Psa 64:7</reference>, a planned plan = a cunningly wrought out plan; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, and Vitringa thereto: grounded = firm, grounding), Ewald, §313c. The reckoning moves in the contrasts of littleness to power, and of greatness to prudence. The unfolding of the ארבעה [four] begins with the הנּמלים [the ants] and שׁפנּים [conies], subject conceptions with apposit. joined; 26a, at least in the indetermination of the subject, cannot be a declaration. Regarding the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. as the expression, not of a causal, but of a contrasted connection, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ewald, §342, 1a. The ants are called עם, and they deserve this name, for they truly form communities with well-ordered economy; but, besides, the ancients took delight in speaking of the various classes of animals as peoples and states.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Walter von der Vogelweide</hi>, edited by Lachmann, p. 8f.</note> <div eID="gen11970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11971" type="x-p"/> That which is said, 25b, as also <reference osisRef="Prov.6.8">Pro 6:8</reference>, is not to be understood of stores laid up for the winter. For the ants are torpid for the most part in winter; but certainly the summer is their time for labour, when the labourers gather together food, and feed in a truly motherly way the helpless. שׁפן, translated arbitrarily in the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. by ἐχῖνοι, in the lxx by χοιρογρύλλιοι, by the Syr. and Targ. here and at Ps 104 by חגס, and by Jerome by <hi type="italic">lepusculus</hi> (cf. λαγίδιον), both of which names, here to be understood after a prevailing Jewish opinion, denote the <hi type="italic">Caninichen</hi><note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">kaninchen</hi> as well as the <hi type="italic">klippdachs</hi> [cliff-badgers] may be meant, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.5">Lev 11:5</reference> (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.7">Deu 14:7</reference>); neither of these belong to the <hi type="italic">bisulca</hi>, nor yet, it is true, to the ruminants, though to the ancients (as was the case also with hares) they seemed to do. The <hi type="italic">klippdach</hi> is still, in Egypt and Syria, regarded as unclean.</note> (Luther), Latin <hi type="italic">cuniculus</hi> (κόνικλος), is not the <hi type="italic">kaninchen</hi> [rabbit], nor the marmot, χοιρογρύλλιος (C. B. Michaelis, Ziegler, and others); this is called in Arab. yarbuw'; but שׁפן is the wabr, which in South Arab. is called thufun, or rather thafan, viz., the <hi type="italic">klippdachs</hi> (<hi type="italic">hyrax syriacus</hi>), like the marmot, which lives in societies and dwells in the clefts of the mountains, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at the Kedron, the Dead Sea, and at Sinai (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Knobel on <reference osisRef="Lev.11.5">Lev 11:5</reference>; cf. Brehm’s <hi type="italic">Thierleben</hi>, ii. p. 721ff., the <hi type="italic">Illustrirte Zeitung</hi>, 1868, Nr. 1290). The <hi type="italic">klippdachs</hi> are a weak little people, and yet with their weakness they unite the wisdom that they establish themselves among the rocks. The ants show their wisdom in the organization of labour, here in the arranging of inaccessible dwellings.
entries.5b7c222428eb7b7f9c433bfaf5eb65ef2623bdcb: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.29-Prov.30.31">Pro 30:29-31</reference> <div eID="gen11973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11974" type="x-p"/> Another numerical proverb with the cipher 4 = 3 + 1: 29 Three things are of stately walk,      And four of stately going: 30 The lion, the hero among beasts,      And that turneth back before nothing; 31 The swift-loined, also the goat;      And a king with whom is the calling out of the host. <div eID="gen11974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11975" type="x-p"/> Regarding היטיב with <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. following (the segolated <hi type="italic">n. actionis</hi> צעד is of equal force with an <hi type="italic">inf</hi>.), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 15:2.<note placement="foot">In 29a, after Norzi, מיטיבי, and in 29b, מיטבי, is to be written, and this is required by the little Masora to <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.31">1Sa 25:31</reference>, the great, to <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.33">Eze 33:33</reference>, and also the Erfurt little Masora to the passage before us.</note> <div eID="gen11975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11976" type="x-p"/> The relation of the members of the sentence in 30a is like that in 25a and 26a: subj. and apposit., which there, as here, is continued in a verbal clause which appears to us as relative. It deserves to be here remarked that לישׁ, as the name for a lion, occurs only here and at <reference osisRef="Job.4.11">Job 4:11</reference>, and in the description of the Sinai wilderness, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>; in Arab. it is layth, Aram. לית, and belongs to the Arameo-Arab. dialect of this language; the lxx and Syr. translate it “the young lion;” the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. excellently, by the epic λῖς. בּבּהמה has the article only to denote the genus, viz., of the beasts, and particularly the four-footed beasts. What is said in 30b (cf. with the expression, <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job 39:22</reference>) is described in Isa 30:4. The two other beasts which distinguish themselves by their stately going are in 31a only briefly named. But we are not in the condition of the readers of this Book of Proverbs, who needed only to hear the designation זרזיר מתנים at once to know what beast was meant. Certainly זרזיר, as the name for a beast, is not altogether unknown in the post-bibl. Heb. “In the days of Rabbi Chija (the great teacher who came from Babylon to the Academy of Sepphoris), as is narrated in <hi type="italic">Bereschith rabba</hi>, sect. 65, a zarzir flew to the land of Israel, and it was brought to him with the question whether it were eatable. Go, said he, place it on the roof! Then came an Egyptian raven and lighted down beside it. See, said Chija, it is unclean, for it belongs to the genus of the ravens, which is unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.15">Lev 11:15</reference>). From this circumstance there arose the proverb: The raven goes to the zarzir because it belongs to his own tribe.”<note placement="foot">This “like draws to like” in the form: “not in vain goes the raven to the zarzir, it belongs just to its own tribe,” came to be often employed, <hi type="italic">Chullin</hi> 65a, <hi type="italic">Baba Kamma</hi> 92b. Plantavitius has it, Tendlau more at large, <hi type="italic">Sprichwörter, u.s.w</hi>., Nr. 577.</note> <div eID="gen11976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11977" type="x-p"/> Also the Jer. <hi type="italic">Rosch ha-schane</hi>, Halacha 3: “It is the manner of the world that one seeks to assist his zarzir, and another his zarzir, to obtain the victory;” and <hi type="italic">Midrash Echa</hi> v. 1, according to which it is the custom of the world, that one who has a large and a little zarzir in his house, is wont to treat the little one sparingly, so that in the case of the large one being killed, he might not need to buy another. According to this, the zarzir is a pugnacious animal, which also the proverb <hi type="italic">Bereschith rabba</hi>, c. 75, confirms: two zarzir do not sleep on one board; and one makes use of his for contests like cock-fights. According to this, the זרזיר is a bird, and that of the species of the raven; after Rashi, the <hi type="italic">étourneau</hi>, the starling, which is confirmed by the Arab. zurzur (vulgar Arab. zarzur), the common name of starlings (cf. Syr. zarzizo, under zrz of Castelli). But for the passage before us, we cannot regard this as important, for why is the starling fully named זרזיר מתנים? To this question Kimchi has already remarked that he knows no answer for it. Only, perhaps, the grave magpie (<hi type="italic">corvus pica</hi>), strutting with upraised tail, might be called <hi type="italic">succinctus lumbos</hi>, if מתנים can at all be used here of a bird. At the earliest, this might possibly be used of a cock, which the later Heb. named directly גּבר, because of its manly demeanour; most old translators so understand it. The lxx translates, omitting the loins, by ἀλέκτωρ ἐμπεριπατῶν θηλείαις εὔψυχος, according to which the Syr. and Targ.: like the cock which struts about proudly among the hens;<note placement="foot">Regarding the Targum Text, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Levy under אבּכא and זרכּל. The expression דּמזדּרז (who is girded, and shows himself as such) is not unsuitable.</note> <div eID="gen11977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11978" type="x-p"/> Aquila and Theodotion: ἀλέκτωρ (ἀλεκτρυὼν) νώτου; The Quinta: ἀλέκτωρ ὀσφύος; Jezome: <hi type="italic">gallus succinctus lumbos</hi>. Ṣarṣar (not ṣirṣir, as Hitzig vocalizes) is in Arab. a name for a cock, from ṣarṣara, to crow, an onomatopoeia. But the Heb. זרזיר, as the name of a bird, signifies, as the Talmud proves on the ground of that history, not a cock, but a bird of the raven order, whether a starling, a crow, or a magpie. And if this name of a <hi type="italic">corvinus</hi> is formed from the <hi type="italic">onomatopoeia</hi> זרזר, the weaker form of that (Arab.) ṣarṣar, then מתנים, which, for זרזיר, requires the verbal root זרז, to girdle, is not wholly appropriate; and how strangely would the three animals be mingled together, if between לישׁ and תישׁ, the two four-footed animals, a bird were placed! If, as is to be expected, the “<hi type="italic">Lendenumgürtete</hi>” [the one girded about the loins = זרזיר מתנים] be a four-footed animal, then it lies near, with C. B. Michaelis and Ziegler, after Ludolf's<note placement="foot">Ludolf gave, in his <hi type="italic">Hist. Aethiop</hi>. i. 10, and <hi type="italic">Commentarius</hi>, p. 150, only a description of the <hi type="italic">Zecora</hi>, without combining therewith זרזיר; but <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Joh. Dietr. Winckler’s <hi type="italic">Theol. u. Philol. Abhand</hi>. i. (1755) p. 33ff.: “A nearer explanation of what is to be understood by זרזיר מתנים, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.31">Pro 30:31</reference>, along with a statement from a hitherto unpublished correspondence between the learned philologists Hiob Ludolf and Matthai Leydecker, a Reformed preacher in Batavia.” With Ludolf, Joh. Simonis also, in the Arcanum Formarum (1735), p. 687f., decides in favour of the zebra.</note> example, to think of the zebra, the South African wild ass. But this animal lay beyond the sphere of the author’s observation, and perhaps also of his knowledge, and at the same time of that of the Israelitish readers of this Book of Proverbs; and the dark-brown cross stripes on a white ground, by which the zebra is distinguished, extend not merely to its limbs, but over the whole body, and particularly over the front of the body. It would be more tenable to think of the leopard, with its black round spots, or the tiger, with dark stripes; but the name זרזיר מתנים scarcely refers to the colour of the hair, since one has to understand it after the Aram. זרז חרציהּ = שׁנּס מתניו, 1Ki 18:46, or אחר חלציו, <reference osisRef="Job.38.3">Job 38:3</reference>, and thus of an activity, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, strength and swiftness, depending on the condition of the loins. Those who, with Kimchi, think that the נמר [leopard] is thus named, ground their view, not on this, that it has rings or stripes round its legs, but on this, that it דק מתנים וחזק במתניו. But this beast has certainly its definite name; but a fundamental supposition entering into every attempt at an explanation is this, that זרזיר מתנים, as well as לישׁ and תישׁ, is the proper name of a beast, not a descriptive attribute. Therefore the opinion of Rosse, which Bochart has skilfully established in the <hi type="italic">Hierozoicon</hi>, does not recommend itself, for he only suggests, for choice, to understand the name, “the girded about the loins,” in the proper sense of straps and clasps around and on the loins (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Gesenius, Fleischer, Hitzig), or of strength, in the sense of the Arab. habuwk, the firmly-bound = compact, or ṣamm alṣlab, the girded loin (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Muntinghe). Schultens connects together both references: <hi type="italic">Utrumque jungas licet</hi>. That the by-name fits the horse, particularly the war-horse, is undeniable; one would have to refer it, with Mühlau, to the slender structure, the thin flanks, which are reckoned among the requisites of a beautiful horse.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Ahlwardt, <hi type="italic">Chalef elahmar’s Qasside</hi> (1859), and the interpretation of the description of the horse contained therein, p. 210ff.</note> <div eID="gen11978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11979" type="x-p"/> But if <hi type="italic">succinctus lumbos</hi> were a by-name of a horse, why did not the author at once say סוס זרזיר מתנים? We shall give the preference to the opinion, according to which the expression, “girt about the loins” = “with strong loins,” or “with slender limbs,” is not the by-name, but the proper name of the animal. This may be said of the hunting-hound, <hi type="italic">lévrier</hi> (according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., incorrectly translating מתנים: λαγῳοκύων ψοιῶν),<note placement="foot">Thus reads Schleusner, <hi type="italic">Opusc. Crit</hi>. p. 318, and refers it to the horse: <hi type="italic">nam solebant equos figuris quibusdam notare et quasi sigillare</hi>.</note> which Kimchi ranks in the first place. Luther, by his translation, <hi type="italic">Ein Wind</hi> = <hi type="italic">Windhund</hi> [greyhound], of good limbs, has given the right direction to this opinion. Melanchton, Lavater, Mercier, Geier, and others, follow him; and, among the moderns, so also do Ewald and Böttcher (also Bertheau and Stuart), which latter supposes that before זרזיר מתנים there originally stood כבל, which afterwards disappeared. But why should the greyhound not at once be called זרזיר מתנים? We call the smaller variety of this dog the <hi type="italic">Windspiel</hi> [greyhound]; and by this name we think on a hound, without saying <hi type="italic">Windspielhund</hi>. The name זרזיר מתנים (Symmachus excellently: περιεσφιγμένος, not περιεσφραγισμένος, τὴν ὀσφύν, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, strongly bound in the limbs) is fitted at once to suggest to us this almost restless, slender animal, with its high, thin, nimble limbs. The verbal stem זרר (Arab.) zarr, signifies to press together, to knit together; the reduplicative form זרזר, to bind firmly together, whence זרזיר, firmly bound together, referred to the limbs as designating a natural property (Ewald, §158a): of straight and easily-moveable legs.<note placement="foot">The Aram. זרז is shortened from זרזר, as כּרך from כּרכּר; the particip. adj. זריז signifies nimble, swift, eager, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pesachim</hi> 4a: “the zealous obey the commandment - as soon as possible hasten to fulfil it.”</note> <div eID="gen11979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11980" type="x-p"/> The hunting-hound (<hi type="italic">salâki</hi> or <hi type="italic">salûki</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, coming from Seleucia) is celebrated by the Arab. poets as much as the hunting-horse.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Ahlwardt, <hi type="italic">Chalef elahmar’s Qasside</hi>, p. 205f.</note> <div eID="gen11980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11981" type="x-p"/> The name כּלב, though not superfluous, the author ought certainly to have avoided, because it does not sound well in the Heb. collocation of words. <div eID="gen11981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11982" type="x-p"/> There now follows תישׁ, a goat, and that not the ram (Jerome, Luther), which is called איל, but the he-goat, which bears this name, as Schultens has already recognised, from its pushing, as it is also called עתּוּד, as <hi type="italic">paratus ad pugnam</hi>; the two names appear to be only provincially different; שׂעיר, on the contrary, is the old he-goat, as shaggy; and צפיר also perhaps denotes it, as Schultens supposes, with twisted, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, curled hair (<hi type="italic">tortipilus</hi>). In Arab. tays denotes the he-goat as well as the roebuck and the gazelle, and that at full growth. The lxx (the Syr. and Targ., which is to be emended after the Syr.) is certainly right, for it understands the leading goat: καὶ τράγος ἡγούμενος αἰπολίου. The text, however, has not ותישׁ, but או תישׁ, ἢ τράγος (Aquila, Theodotion, Quinta, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.). Böttcher is astonished that Hitzig did not take hold of this או, and conjectures תּאו־תישׁ, which should mean a “gazelle-goat” (Mühlau: <hi type="italic">dorcas mas</hi>). But it is too bold to introduce here תּאו (תּוא), which is only twice named in the O.T., and תאו־תישׁ for תּאו זכר is not the Heb. style; and besides, the setting aside of או has a harsh <hi type="italic">asyndeton</hi> for its consequence, which bears evidence to the appearance that תאו and תישׁ are two different animals. And is the או then so objectionable? More wonderful still must Sol 2:9 appear to us. If the author enumerated the four of stately going on his fingers, he would certainly have said ותישׁ. By או he communicates to the hearer, setting before him another figure, how there in the Song Sulamith’s fancy passed from one object to another. <div eID="gen11982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11983" type="x-p"/> To the lion, the king of the animal world, the king אלקוּם עמּו corresponds. This אלקום Hitzig regards as mutilated from אלהים (which was both written and pronounced as אלקום by the Jews, so as to conceal the true sound of the name of God) - which is untenable, for this reason, that this religious conclusion [“A king with whom God is”] accords badly with the secular character of this proverb. Geiger (<hi type="italic">Urschrift</hi>, p. 62ff.) translates: “and King Alkimos corresponding to it (the lustful and daring goat)” - he makes the harmless proverb into a <hi type="italic">ludibrium</hi> from the time of the Maccabeo-Syrian war. The lxx, which the Syr. and Targ. follow, translates καὶ βασιλεὺς δημηγορῶν ἐν ἔθνει; it appears to have changed אלקום עמו into קם אל עמו (standing with his people and haranguing them), like the Quinta: καὶ βας. ἀναστὰς (ὃς ἀνέστη) ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ. Ziegler and Böttcher also, reading עמּו and אל without any transposition, get ומלך אל־קוּם עמּו t, which the former translates: “a king with the presence of his people;” the latter, “a king with the setting up of his people,” - not accordant with the thought, for the king should be brought forward as מיטיב לכת. For the same reason, Kimchi’s explanation is not suitable: a king with whom is no resistance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, against whom no one can rank himself (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also Immanuel); or more specially, but not better: who has no successor of his race (according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἀδιάδεκτος ξὺν ἑαυτῷ). Rather this explanation commends itself: a king with whom (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in war with whom) is no resistance. Thus Jerome and Luther: against whom no one dare place himself; thus Rashi, Aben Ezra, Ralbag (שׁאין תקומה עמו), Ahron b. Josef (קום = ἀντίστασις), Arama, and others; thus also Schultens, Fleischer (<hi type="italic">adversus quem nemo consistere audet</hi>), Ewald, Bertheau, Elster, Stuart, and others. But this connection of אל with the infin. is not Heb.; and if the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, xii. 28, has coined the expression אל־מות for the idea of “immortality,” then certainly it does not express the idea of resistlessness by so bold a <hi type="italic">quasi compositum</hi>. But this boldness is also there mitigated, for יהי is supplied after אל, which is not here practicable with קוּם, which is not a subst. like מות. Pocock in the <hi type="italic">Spec. historiae Arabum</hi>, and Castellus in the <hi type="italic">Lex. Heptaglotton</hi> (not Castellio, as the word is printed by Zöckler), have recognised in אלקום the Arab. âlkawm; Schultens gives the lxx the honour of this recognition, for he regards their translation as a paraphrase of ὁ δῆμος μετ ̓ αὐτοῦ. Bertheau thinks that it ought to be in Arab. kawmuhu, but אלקום עמו = âlkawhu ma'ahu is perfectly correct, âlkawhu is the summons or the <hi type="italic">Heerbann</hi> = <hi type="italic">arriere-ban</hi>;<note placement="foot">Wetzstein’s <hi type="italic">Ausgewählte Inschriften</hi>, p. 355: “The word ḳawm signifies people, not in the sense of <hi type="italic">populus</hi>, but in the sense of the Heb. קים (<reference osisRef="Job.24.7">Job 24:7</reference>) = muḳawim abrajul, he who breaks with or against any one.” Incorrect in Gesenius-Dietrich’s <hi type="italic">Heb. Wörterbuch</hi>.</note> in North Africa they speak in their language in the same sense of the <hi type="italic">Gums</hi>. This explanation of אלקום, from the Arab. Dachselt (<hi type="italic">rex cum satellitio suo</hi>), Diedrichs in his Arab.-Syr. <hi type="italic">Spicilegium</hi> (1777), Umbreit, Gesenius, and Vaihinger, have recognised, and Mühlau has anew confirmed it at length. Hitzig, on the contrary, remarks that if Agur wrote on Arab. territory, we could be contented with the Arab. appellative, but not with the article, which in words like אלגּבישׁ and אלמגּים is no longer of force as an art., but is an integ. component part of the word. We think that it is with אלקום exactly as with other words descriptive of lordship, and the many similar that have passed over into the Spanish language; the word is taken over along with the article, without requiring the Heb. listener to take the art. as such, although he certainly felt it better than we do, when we say “<hi type="italic">das Alkoran</hi>” [the Alcoran], “<hi type="italic">das Alcohol</hi>,” and the like. Blau also, in his <hi type="italic">Gesch. der Arab. Substantiv-Determ</hi>.,<note placement="foot">In the “<hi type="italic">Alt-arab. Sprachstudien</hi>,” <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr</hi>. xxv. 539f.</note> regards it as certain that Agur borrowed this אלקום from the idiom of the Arabians, among whom he lived, and heard it constantly spoken. By this explanation we first reach a correspondence between what is announced in lines first and second and line sixth. A king as such is certainly not “comely in going;” he can sit upon his throne, and especially as δημηγορῶν will he sit (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.21">Act 12:21</reference>) and not stand. But the majesty of his going shows itself when he marches at the head of those who have risen up at his summons to war. Then he is for the army what the תישׁ he-goat is for the flock. The או, preferred to ו, draws close together the רישׁ e and the king (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Isa 14:9</reference>).
entries.a42974aa68e06edf74fe933f4f846c44c16e6213: <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32-Prov.30.33">Pro 30:32-33</reference> <div eID="gen11983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11984" type="x-p"/> Another proverb, the last of Agur’s “Words” which exhorts to thoughtful, discreet demeanour, here follows the proverb of self-conscious, grave deportment: 32 If thou art foolish in that thou exaltest thyself,      Or in devising, - put thy hand to thy mouth! 33 For the pressure on milk bringeth forth butter,      And pressure on the nose bringeth forth blood,      And pressure on sensibility bringeth forth altercation. <div eID="gen11984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11985" type="x-p"/> Löwenstein translates <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Pro 30:32</reference> : <div eID="gen11985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11986" type="x-p"/> Art thou despicable, it is by boasting; <div eID="gen11986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11987" type="x-p"/> Art thou prudent, then hold thy hand on thy mouth. <div eID="gen11987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11988" type="x-p"/> But if זמם denotes reflection and deliberation, then נבל, as its opposite, denotes unreflecting, foolish conduct. Then בּהתנשּׂא ne by boasting is not to be regarded as a consequent (thus it happens by lifting thyself up; or: it is connected with boasting); by this construction also, אם־נבלתּ must be accented with <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi>, not with <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>. Otherwise Euchel: <div eID="gen11988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11989" type="x-p"/> Hast thou become offensive through pride, <div eID="gen11989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11990" type="x-p"/> Or seems it so to thee, - lay thy hand to thy mouth. <div eID="gen11990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11991" type="x-p"/> The thought is appropriate,<note placement="foot">Yet the Talmud, <hi type="italic">Nidda</hi> 27a, derives another moral rule from this proverb, for it interprets זמם in the sense of זמם = חסם, to tie up, to bridle, to shut up, but אם נבלת in the sense of “if thou hast made thyself despicable,” as Löwenstein has done.</note> but נבלתּ for נבּלתּ is more than improbable; נבל, thus absolutely taken in an ethical connection, is certainly related to נבל, as כּסל, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.8">Jer 10:8</reference>, to כּסיל. The prevailing mode of explanation is adopted by Fleischer: <hi type="italic">si stulta arrogantia elatus fueris et si quid durius</hi> (<hi type="italic">in alios</hi>) <hi type="italic">mente conceperis, manum ori impone</hi>; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, if thou arrogantly, and with offensive words, wilt strive with others, then keep thyself back, and say not what thou hast in thy mind. But while מזמּה and מזמּות denote intrigues, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.17">Pro 14:17</reference>, as well as plans and considerations, זמם has never by itself alone the sense of <hi type="italic">meditari mala</hi>; at <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12">Psa 37:12</reference>, also with ל of the object at which the evil devices aim. Then for ואם ... אם (Arab. ân ... wân) there is the supposition of a correlative relation, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 1Ki 20:18; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference>, by which at the same time זמּות is obviously thought of as a contrast to נבלתּ. This contrast excludes<note placement="foot">The Arab. signification, to become proud, is a <hi type="italic">nüance</hi> of the primary signification, to hold erect - viz. the head - as when the rider draws up the head of a camel by means of the halter (Arab. zamam).</note> for זמות not only the sense of <hi type="italic">mala moliri</hi> (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also Mühlau), but also the sense of the Arab. zamm, <hi type="italic">superbire</hi> (Schultens). Hitzig has the right determination of the relation of the members of the sentence and the ideas: if thou art irrational in ebullition of temper and in thought - thy hand to thy mouth!
