But התנשּׂא has neither here nor elsewhere the meaning of התעבּר (to be out of oneself with anger); it signifies everywhere to elevate or exalt oneself, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, rightly or wrongly to make much of oneself. There are cases where a man, who raises himself above others, appears as a fool, and indeed acts foolishly; but there are also other cases, when the despised has a reason and an object for vindicating his superiority, his repute, his just claim: when, as we say, he places himself in his right position, and assumes importance; the poet here recommends, to the one as well as to the other, silence. The rule that silence is gold has its exceptions, but here also it is held valid as a rule. Luther and others interpret the <hi type="italic">perfecta</hi> as looking back: “hast thou become a fool and ascended too high and intended evil, then lay thy hand on thy mouth.” But the reason in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.33">Pro 30:33</reference> does not accord with this rendering, for when that has been done, the occasion for hatred is already given; but the proverb designs to warn against the stirring up of hatred by the reclaiming of personal pretensions. The <hi type="italic">perfecta</hi>, therefore, are to be interpreted as at <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">Deu 32:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.15">Job 9:15</reference>, as the expression of the abstract present; or better, as at <reference osisRef="Job.9.16">Job 9:16</reference>, as the expression of the <hi type="italic">fut. exactum</hi>: if thou wouldest have acted foolishly, since thou walkest proudly, or if thou hadst (before) thought of it (Aquila, Theodotion: καὶ ἐὰν ἐννοηθῇς) - the hand on thy mouth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, let it alone, be silent rather (expression as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>; Jdg 18:19; <reference osisRef="Job.40.4">Job 40:4</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. best: εἴπερ ἐμώρανας ἐν τῷ ἐπαίρεσθαι καὶ εἴπερ ἐλογίσω, χεὶρ τῷ στόματι. When we have now interpreted התנשׂא, not of the rising up of anger, we do not also, with Hitzig, interpret the dual of the two snorting noses - viz. of the double anger, that of him who provokes to anger, and that of him who is made angry - but אפּים denotes the two nostrils of one and the same person, and, figuratively, snorting or anger. Pressure against the nose is designated ומיץ־אף, ἐκμύζησις (ἐκπίεσις) μυκτῆρος (write ומיץ־אף, with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, with the long tone, after <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>-<hi type="italic">Setzung</hi>, §11, 9, 12), and מיץ אפּים, ἐκμύζησις θυμοῦ (Theodotion), with reference to the proper meaning of אפים, pressure to anger, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to the stirring up and strengthening of anger. The nose of him who raises himself up comes into view, in so far as, with such self-estimation, sneering, snuffling scorn (μυκτηρίζειν) easily connects itself; but this view of מתנשׂא is not here spoken of.  <chapter eID="Prov.30"/> <div eID="gen11991" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 THe words of Agur the son of Jakeh <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">A Person so called as appears from the designation of his own and his Fathers Name, who lived either in <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s time, or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther afterwards<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and was famous in his Generation for Wisdom, and Prety, and Prophecy, and therefore his Proverbs were thought fit to be added to those of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> either by those men of <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zekiah,</ns0:hi> mentioned Ch. 25. 1. or by some other. But that this should be meant of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> may easily be supposed, but cannot be proved, nor is it probable, as being contrary both to the Style of the whole Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, and to the matter of some part of it, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7, 8, 9. which agrees not to <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> and to the Laws of good Interpretation, one of which is that all words should be taken in their most natural and proper sence, when there is no evidence, nor necessity of under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing them improperly and figuratively, which is the present case.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the prophecy <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Prophetical instruction; for as the Prophets were publick Preachers as well as Foretellers of things to come, so their Sermons, no less than their Predictions, are commonly called their <ns0:hi>Prophesies.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Two Friends or Disciples, and contemporaries of <ns0:hi>Agur,</ns0:hi> called by those Names, who having a great and just opinion of his Wisdom, desired his instructions. Others, <ns0:hi>concerning</ns0:hi> Ithiel and <ns0:hi>Ucal;</ns0:hi> which they understand of Christ called <ns0:hi>Ithiel,</ns0:hi> which signifies <ns0:hi>God with me,</ns0:hi> and answers to <ns0:hi>Immanuel,</ns0:hi> which is <ns0:hi>God with us,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ucal,</ns0:hi> which signifies <ns0:hi>power</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>prevalency.</ns0:hi> But if he had meant this of Christ, why should he design him by such obscure and ambiguous Names, as if he would not be understood? Why did he not call him by the Name of <ns0:hi>Shilo</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> or some other Scripture Title belonging and ascribed to him? Besides, this Interpretation agrees not with the contents of this Chapter, wherein there is onely a short and occasional mention of Christ, but the Chapter consists in a manner wholly of counsels and Sentences of a quite other kind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Surely I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> more brutish than <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>a great Man.</ns0:hi> Ch. 8, 4.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> man, and have not the understanding of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> a mean Man.</ns0:note> a man <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">You come to me with a great opinion of my Wisdom, and you expect that I should inform and instruct you in all things, yea even in the greatest Mysteries: but you are much mistaken in me; I am as ignorant and foolish as other men generally are, yea more than many others. Which he utters either 1. from a deep sense of the common corruption of humane Nature, and of the blindness of mens Minds in things concerning God and their own duty, and of the necessity of instruction from God's Word and of illumination from his Spirit, without which they can never understand these matters. Or 2. from a modest and humble apprehension of his own ignorance, which hath extorted such like expressions even from Heathen Philosophers; whence <ns0:hi>Pythagoras</ns0:hi> rejected the Title of a <ns0:hi>wise Man</ns0:hi> when it was ascribed to him; and <ns0:hi>Socrates,</ns0:hi> though reputed the wisest Man of his Age, professed that he <ns0:hi>knew nothing but this that he knew nothing.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 I neither learned wisdom <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I have not been taught in the Schools of Wisdom, as the Sons of Prophets were, but must own my self to be an unlearned Man, as the Prophet <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 7. 14, 15. Or, I have not learned it, neither by my own understanding and study, nor by the help of other men.</ns0:note>, nor <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> know.</ns0:note> have the know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of the holy <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. of the holy Angels, who are called <ns0:hi>Holy</ns0:hi> by way of eminency, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 2. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 15. 15. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 4. 13, 17, 23. & 8. 13.                   <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 19. 10<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Eccl. 10. 7.</ns0:note> For a servant when he reigneth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">When he is advanced to great Power and Dignity; for such an one is ignorant and unfit for his place, and therefore commits many errours, he is poor, and therefore an insatiable oppressor, according to <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 28. 3. he is proud and imperious, and being ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligned and hated by others, he is provoked to hate them, and to be injurious and cruel to them.</ns0:note>, and a fool <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">A conceited and wilful fool, or an obstinately wicked man.</ns0:note> when he is filled with meat <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either 1. When he is glutted with meat or drink, which dulls mens Reason, and heats their Blood, and stirs them up to many insolencies. Or rather 2. When he abounds in Wealth, which in that case is like a Sword in a mad mans hand, being an instrument and occasion of innumerable wickednesses and mischiefs, as appears from common experi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:543" />23 For an odious <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Proud, and perverse, and full of hateful and offensive qualities.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>woman</ns0:hi> when she is married <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For then she displayeth, and exerciseth all those ill humours, which before for her own ends she concealed, then she is puffed up, and imperious, and becomes intollerable to her own Family, and to her Relations and Neighbours.</ns0:note>, and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That possesseth her Estate, either by the gift of her Mistress, into whose Favour she had insinuated her self by her cunning and officious car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage: or rather by the marriage of her Master, which great and sudden change transports her beside her self, and makes her in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sufferably proud, and scornful, and injurious to all that converse with her.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 There be four <ns0:hi>things which are</ns0:hi> little upon the earth, but they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> wise, made wise.</ns0:note> exceeding wise <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Comparatively to other brute Creatures. They act very wise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly and providently, not from any reason which they have, but by the direction of divine Providence, which secretly guides them to do those things for their own preservation which are most agreea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to the rules of Wisdom. The design of this observation is ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. To commend Wisdom to us, and to teach us to imitate the Providence of these Creatures, as we are provoked to imitate their diligence, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 6. 6. Or 2. To keep us from being proud<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly conceited of our own Wisdom, because we are either equalled or exceeded therein by the unreasonable Creatures in the wise con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duct of their affairs. Or 3. To direct us to whom to resort for Wisdom when we want and desire it, even to that God who is able to inspire Wisdom even into the brute Creatures.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 6. 6, &c.</ns0:note> The ants <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> a people <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which title is oft given to the unreasonable Creatures both in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 1. 6. & 2. 2. and in <ns0:hi>Homer,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Virgil</ns0:hi> and di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers other Authors.</ns0:note> not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Of which see on <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 6. 6, 7, 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 104. 18.</ns0:note> The conies <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In rocky ground, or in the holes of Rocks for their safety, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst their too potent Enemies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 The locusts have no king <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To rule and order them.</ns0:note>, yet go they forth all of them <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> gather<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed together.</ns0:note> by bands <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In great numbers, and in seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral companies, and in exact order, as is observed in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 5. & 7. 12. <ns0:hi>Ioel.</ns0:hi> 1. 7. & 2. 7. and by other Writers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 The spider taketh hold <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of the thread which she spins out of her own bowels.</ns0:note> with her hands <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With her Legs which he calls <ns0:hi>Hands,</ns0:hi> because they serve her for the same purpose, to do her work, to weave her web, and to catch Gnats or Flies, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and is in kings palaces <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Is not only in poor Cottages, but many times in Palaces also, where she makes a shift to keep her abode, notwith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing all the care and pains which is taken to sweep and cleanse it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 There be three <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> which go well, yea, four are comely in going <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That walk decently, and with great alacrity and courage; which are here commended to us to imitate in the management of our affairs.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 A lion <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> is strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He doth not flee from his pursuers, whether Men or Beasts, but walketh away with a slow and Majestick pace, as is observed by <ns0:hi>Aristotle,</ns0:hi> and many others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 A <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Horse.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> girt in the loins.</ns0:note> grey-hound <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Called in Hebrew, <ns0:hi>girt in the loins,</ns0:hi> either because its loins are slender, and as it were girt up into a little compass, and right or well trussed up: or because of its great agility and swiftness, for the girding of the loins was used for expedition in going or work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing. Or, as it is rendred by others, <ns0:hi>an Horse,</ns0:hi> to wit, a War<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>horse, having his Armour girt about him, and marching to the battle, which he doth with great Majesty and Courage, as God himself observes at large, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 39. 19, &c.</ns0:note>, an he-goat <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which marcheth in the head of the flock in grave and stately manner, conducting them with great courage and resolution, and being ready to fight for them, either with beasts or men that oppose him. Whence great Cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains are oft compared to <ns0:hi>he-goats,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 14. 9. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 8. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 8. 5, 21. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 10. 3.</ns0:note> also, and a king, against whom <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no rising up <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A mighty and victorious King, whose power none can withstand, who therefore goeth hither and thither, and proceedeth in his affairs with invincible Courage and Majesty. But this place, with the variation of one Hebrew point, reading <ns0:hi>ammo</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>immo,</ns0:hi> may be rendred, as a very learned man observes, <ns0:hi>a King and his People with him,</ns0:hi> a King when he hath the Hearts and Hands of his People going along with him in his underta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thy self <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either 1. By Rebellion or Sedition against the King last mentioned. Or 2. By Anger or Wrath, of which he speaks in the next verse. But this Verse hath no necessary dependance either upon the foregoing or following Verse. Or 3. Through thy Pride, which makes men carry themselves very foolishly, and scornfully, and injuriously, and is the root of contention, as was observed, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 13. 10.</ns0:note>, or if thou hast thought evil <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Designed any mischief or injury against thy Neighbour.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 21. 5. & 40. 4.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>lay</ns0:hi> thine hand upon thy mouth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, to shut it: Be silent, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 21. 5. & 29. 9. Restrain thy self, do not speak one word, much less do any thing tending to the accomplishment of it: Do not open thy mouth to justifie or excuse it, but silently and seriously consider the evil of it, and repent of it, and do so no more.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth but<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The stirring up of Wrath, either 1. In a mans self towards others, by giving way to Passion, or by fixing his thoughts upon those things which may enflame it. Or 2. In others by repreaches, injuries, or any other provocations.</ns0:note> bringeth forth strife <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Is the cause of many quarrels, and much mischief among men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
